howto.name: How to get compliant with the Utah AI Policy Act

steps.name: Inventory public-facing generative AI
steps.text: List every generative AI system that interacts with a member of the public in Utah, including vendor chatbots and voice agents you did not build.

steps.name: Separate regulated-occupation uses
steps.text: Flag any system operating in a licensed profession — healthcare, legal, accounting, mental health. These owe proactive disclosure, not just disclosure on request.

steps.name: Test the disclosure
steps.text: Ask each system directly whether it is a human. Record the answer verbatim. A system that hedges or stays in character fails this test.

steps.name: Add proactive disclosure where required
steps.text: For regulated-occupation systems, disclose at the start of the interaction without waiting to be asked, and log that the disclosure was shown.

steps.name: Review claims for deception
steps.text: Apply the ordinary consumer protection test to what the AI says. The Act removes any defence that the machine said it, so the standard is the one applied to your employees.

steps.name: Consider the mitigation programme
steps.text: If you are launching something novel, approach the Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy before deployment rather than after a complaint.

short: Utah requires generative AI to disclose it is not a person, enforced by the Division of Consumer Protection with fines to $2,500 per violation. Amended in 2025 to narrow the general duty to high-risk interactions, with a stricter always-on rule for regulated occupations.
title: Utah AI Policy Act
subtitle: SB 149 (2024), amended by SB 226 and SB 332 (2025)
body_html:
The Utah Artificial Intelligence Policy Act (SB 149) took effect on 1 May 2024 and was the first US state law to require that generative AI tell a person it is not human. It is enforced by the Utah Division of Consumer Protection, sits alongside a new Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy, and was significantly amended in 2025 by SB 226 and SB 332.

What the law actually requires

Two duties, and they are not the same. The first applies to everyone: if a person asks whether they are dealing with a human or a machine, a generative AI system must say clearly that it is not human. As originally passed the duty was broad; the 2025 amendments narrowed it so it bites on high-risk interactions rather than every consumer conversation.

The second duty is stricter and applies to regulated occupations — the professions Utah licenses, including healthcare, law, accountancy and mental health. There, disclosure must be proactive. The AI has to identify itself at the start of the interaction, without waiting to be asked. This is the part most organisations miss: a chatbot triaging patient questions for a licensed clinic is held to a higher standard than the same chatbot selling shoes.

The Act also removes a defence rather than creating a new offence. A business cannot argue that generative AI produced the deceptive statement on its own. If your AI says something that would breach Utah consumer protection law had a human employee said it, you are answerable for it. That is the provision with the widest reach and the least attention.

Who enforces it

The Division of Consumer Protection holds administrative enforcement, with civil penalties up to $2,500 per violation, and the Division can seek injunctive relief and disgorgement. The Attorney General may bring an enforcement action in court. There is no private right of action, so the practical exposure is regulatory rather than class litigation — the opposite of the Illinois BIPA pattern.

The Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy is not an enforcer. It administers a regulatory mitigation programme: a company can enter an agreement with the Office, get tailored rules and reduced penalty exposure while it tests an AI product, and in exchange accepts oversight. It is a sandbox with a signed agreement, and it is the reason to talk to Utah early rather than after a complaint.

Why Utah matters more than its size suggests

Utah did not attempt a risk-tier regime like Colorado or the EU. It took one narrow question — does the person know they are talking to a machine — and answered it with a duty and a fine. That makes it the cheapest state law to comply with and the easiest to breach accidentally, because compliance depends on the behaviour of a chatbot rather than on a governance programme.

It also sets the template several states have since followed. If your disclosure design satisfies Utah for licensed professions, it will usually satisfy the disclosure element of laws elsewhere. The reverse is not true.

What to do about it

Find every generative AI system that speaks to a member of the public. For each, answer three questions: does it disclose when asked, does it disclose proactively where a regulated occupation is involved, and would anything it says be a deceptive practice if an employee had said it. Those three answers are your Utah position. Everything else is documentation.

meta_description: Utah was the first US state to require generative AI to say it is not human. What SB 149 obliges, who the Division of Consumer Protection can fine, and what the 2025 amendments narrowed.
